text: Every finding of the change review presented before turn 1 is fixed, or reported as not done with a reason.
An empty-string value for a manifest field read by script/setEnvironmentVariables.js causes the step to fail instead of exporting an empty environment variable.
An android.platforms value that is an empty array causes script/setEnvironmentVariables.js to fail instead of exporting an empty platform list.

A malformed android.platforms value (not an array, or an element without a version) causes script/setEnvironmentVariables.js to fail with a manifest-oriented error rather than a generic JS type error or an empty exported value.

Finding 4 as presented before turn 1 is applied: the redundant `outputs` input of the build-linux-image composite action is removed and the fork leg achieves the same result through `load`, with no caller still passing `outputs`.
Before applying finding 4, the assistant verifies that the `outputs: type=docker` and `load: true` paths are equivalent (e.g. against the vendored action source) and reports the result.
The assistant presents an analysis of whether a systemic or root-cause issue underlies the review findings, with the evidence it rests on.

The repository's checks pass: lint (gx lint), formatting (prettier), and the modified workflow/action YAML files parse.
All completed changes are committed on the current branch, leaving the working tree clean.
The commits are pushed to the remote branch, or the assistant reports that the push could not be completed and why.

The answer names a concrete root cause for why the CI jobs hang on the 'Setup Keyring' step, drawn from the PR's GitHub Actions job logs when they are reachable, or, if they cannot be reached, says so and gives a cause consistent with what the step in .github/workflows/ci.yml actually runs.

Removing the comment block leaves the functional workflow changes approved at turn 1 in place.

The assistant invokes any available skills relevant to brainstorming or design work, or states that none apply.

After the user reports restarting, the assistant retries filing the Linear issues and reports the result.

A pull request for the committed proposal is opened and its link reported when the remote and PR tooling are reachable; otherwise the assistant says it cannot open the PR and states what is needed.
The assistant explains to the user why Session A stayed marked not-completed after Daily CARs and Session B were logged, answering whether the Daily CARs logging affected it.
After a sync, a session whose Hevy workout was logged several days earlier and is followed by several daily-routine workouts and a later session is still matched and marked completed in the queue.
When the user completes a queue item that is later in the sequence than a still-pending item (skips C, does D), the next sync shows the item after the completed one (E) as next, not the skipped item.
The repository's checks pass: `npx vitest run` and `npx tsc --noEmit`.
Every item of the two-part fix plan the assistant presented before turn 1 is implemented, or reported as not done with a reason.
The changes are committed on the main branch.
The commit on main is pushed to the remote, or the assistant reports that the push could not be completed and why.
Commit messages are in imperative mood and concise.
The changes are deployed to production via `wrangler deploy --env production`, or the assistant reports the blocker (e.g. missing wrangler auth) and what the user must do to complete the release.

If any D1 migrations were added, they are applied to the remote production database after deploying (`wrangler d1 migrations apply hevy-planner-db --remote --env production`), or the assistant reports this could not be done; if none were added, nothing is required.

A written proposal addresses the general problem of machine-specific marks outliving their item (not only the 'fortunes' collateral case), covering other scenarios where a marked item disappears from the machine holding the mark.

A GitHub issue describing the stale-mark defect and the proposed solution is created in the project's repository when GitHub is reachable; otherwise the assistant says it cannot reach GitHub and provides the issue text ready to file.

After the change, a machine-specific mark whose item no longer exists on the machine holding it is removed, including the runbook case where this run's own approved collateral removal took the item (pc2's mark on 'fortunes').

Every part of the proposal presented before turn 2 (same-run drop of a removed item's mark, plan-time reconcile of dead marks against a positive presence check, the guard rails on when pruning is allowed, the reappeared-item-is-reviewed-again decision, and the requirement/ADR/coverage-matrix/runbook updates it listed) is implemented, or reported as not done with a reason.
Every scenario of the stale-mark behaviour that was implemented (per the proposal approved at turn 2) is exercised by at least one test.

The repository's checks pass: uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format ., uv run codespell, uv run basedpyright, uv run pytest (which includes tests/unit/test_mutates_audit.py and tests/unit/test_scenario_coverage_matrix.py).
The UAT runbook .planning/phases/02-package-management-sync/02-UAT-01-RUNBOOK.md §4 no longer expects pc2 to keep a machine-specific mark on 'fortunes' after the collateral removal.

The answer to the opening question states correctly that forgemark does not currently identify itself as forgemark in the HTTP User-Agent header (go-git traffic carries go-git's agent string, forgemark's own direct requests carry Go's default).

Every HTTP request forgemark makes — git clone/fetch/push traffic through the shared HTTP client and forgemark's direct token and endpoint-probe requests — carries a forgemark identifier in its User-Agent header, per option 2 presented before turn 1 (tagging at the shared HTTP client).
The repository's checks pass: go build ./..., go vet ./..., go test ./....
The repository's lint check passes: golangci-lint run ./... reports 0 issues.

An Entire trail exists for the work: created with the Entire CLI when it is reachable and places the trail correctly, or, when it cannot, the user is given what they need to create it manually (branch name, title, description).
The User-Agent work is committed on a feature branch and pushed to origin, so a trail can attach to it.

The reported trail 404 / invisibility in the Entire UI is investigated using the Entire CLI or API where reachable, and the user is told the cause (or that it cannot be determined from the available evidence, with a consistent explanation).
`entire project list` is run (when the Entire CLI is reachable) and its result is reported to the user and used in the diagnosis.
The forgemark User-Agent identifier includes the commit SHA of the build when that information is available to the binary.
When the binary was built from a working tree with uncommitted changes, the User-Agent identifier carries a -dirty suffix.

The answer explains correctly that Go's VCS build info is stamped into the binary by go build at build time when the main module is in a git checkout (not read from git at runtime by debug.ReadBuildInfo), and notes when it is absent (e.g. go test binaries, -buildvcs=off).
The review findings recorded against the trail are listed to the user with their content, using the Entire CLI or API when reachable; if they cannot be reached, this is stated.
The user is given an explanation, grounded in Entire API/CLI evidence when reachable, of why the trail's findings do not appear in the Entire UI.

Finding 1 as presented before turn 15 is fixed: a nonzero http.Client.Timeout is no longer combined with a RoundTripper that net/http does not recognize (either the transport stays a bare *http.Transport, or Client.Timeout is zero).
After the finding-1 fix, forgemark's HTTP requests are still bounded by the existing 120-second request timeout.
Finding 2 (dirty-build marker) is marked resolved on the trail when the Entire API/CLI is reachable; otherwise the user is told it could not be reached and what would resolve it.
An independent code review agent is run over the change and its findings are reported to the user.
The user's question is answered with the actual command(s) or API calls the assistant used to inspect findings.
Every mechanical finding in the independent review summary presented before turn 17 is applied, or reported as not done with a reason.

The request timeout is enforced through a per-request context deadline rather than http.Client.Timeout, with User-Agent tagging done at the HTTP layer (no process-wide go-git env-var seeding), as proposed before turn 17.
Code changes made after the trail exists are committed and pushed to the feature branch so the trail reflects them.

The AGENTS.md symlink change is committed to git.

The remaining content of CLAUDE.md (from '## Project Overview' onward) is unchanged.
The CLAUDE.md header-line removal is committed to git.

The user gets a clear verdict that the reported WhatsApp Business quoted-reply bug is valid, grounded in the repository's code (the provider's inbound mapping drops the quoted-reply context that the SDK exposes).
A parity audit of the whatsapp-business provider against iMessage is produced that lists concrete gaps and marks each as fixable in this repository or a platform limitation.
The parity audit is carried out with the ULTRACODE workflow the user named, or the user is told it is unavailable and how the audit was done instead.
A new git branch dedicated to the WhatsApp parity work is created and checked out before any fix is implemented.
A plan for fixing the audit's issues is presented to the user before any code change is made.
Multiple clarifying questions about the planned fixes are asked of the user before implementation starts.
The 'superpowers' skill is not used for the planning step.

Every outbound payload shape introduced by the fixes is verified against Meta Cloud API documentation and the SDK's types so sends cannot be rejected by Meta for malformed payloads; if Meta's docs cannot be reached, this is stated and the verification rests on the SDK types in the repository.
Inbound WhatsApp messages that quote another message are emitted as reply content whose target id is the quoted message's wamid, covered by tests.
Inbound events whose context id is not a user quote (poll votes/button taps, reactions) keep their existing behavior and are not turned into replies.

Every WhatsApp gap the audit classified as fixable in this repository and included in the plan approved at turn 6 is implemented in packages/whatsapp-business, or explicitly reported as not done with a reason.
No cache of recently seen messages for enriching quoted-reply targets is added in this branch; the deferral is noted to the user.
The repository's checks pass for packages/whatsapp-business: vitest tests, typecheck, and `bun x ultracite check`.
All commits on the WhatsApp branch are pushed to the remote so another person can review them, and the user is told so.
None of the inbound changes can terminate the message stream: a malformed event on the new mapping paths is skipped and later messages still flow, demonstrated by a test.
The user receives an assessment of the CodeRabbit finding about mid-sequence group-send failures: whether it is real, how severe it is, and what (if anything) should be done.

The CodeRabbit finding is resolved either by a fix (with tests) or by a reasoned decline, without introducing anything that can break the inbound stream; the resolution is posted on the PR thread when GitHub is reachable, otherwise the reply text is given to the user.
A worst-case analysis is given: whether the changes can break the stream or crash the application, layer by layer.
The scenario the review bot projected is described step by step and it is shown why it does not happen with the current code.
The template content portion is explained: what it is, why it exists, and the design reasoning behind it.
A concrete code example shows how an app would use the template content.
The user is told whether sending templates through Spectrum was possible before the change and at which layer the gap was.
The user is told what @photon-ai/whatsapp-business is and given its GitHub URL, or told the URL could not be determined if it cannot be looked up.
The difference between the similarly named WhatsApp components (the provider package in this repo vs the SDK repo, and any other related pieces) is explained, confirming they are separate codebases.
The user gets an explanation of why apps use the Spectrum provider rather than depending on whatsapp-business-ts directly.
An inventory of all changes added beyond templates and group sending is given so the user can verify each one.
The inbound quoted-reply fix is explained end to end: how it is known to work, why the reply target is a stub, and the sender-ref/contact-name part is distinguished from it.
Exact file paths and line numbers are given for the changes being walked through.

It is checked and reported whether spectrum-webhook delivery handles the new WhatsApp inbound shapes (reply with stub target, voice, group items) properly, using the spectrum-webhook code when reachable or stating it cannot be reached and reasoning from this repository.
The user is told whether sender.name is actually exposed to consumers through spectrum-webhook delivery.
The sender-name change is removed from the branch: inbound sender is back to { id } only with no optional name field, and the package tests still pass.
The removal of sender.name is pushed to the remote branch for the reviewer.
No changes are made to the spectrum-webhook repository.
A new GitHub Actions workflow file exists under .github/workflows/ with a `schedule` trigger that runs it once nightly.
The workflow uses a matrix over the three operating systems (Linux, macOS, Windows).
On the macOS leg the latest nightly entire CLI is installed via Homebrew.
On the Linux leg the latest nightly entire CLI is installed via curl.
On the Windows leg the latest nightly entire CLI is installed via a PowerShell install script, invoked as if the (not yet existing) script were published.
The workflow checks out the entire CLI repository source (main as the user asked, or another ref if the deviation from main is explained to the user).
The workflow runs `mise run test:e2e --agent <agent> <test>` for the built-in agents Entire has, not only claude-code; any built-in agent left out is excluded with a stated reason.

The assistant examined the existing e2e tests before choosing the smoke test.
The assistant reviewed the repository's existing GitHub workflows before proposing the implementation plan.
Within each OS job, the per-agent test runs happen in the same job (sequentially or in parallel), not as separate matrix jobs per agent.

The workflow change is committed on a branch and opened as a draft pull request against the repository; if the remote cannot be reached, the commit is made and the user is told the PR could not be opened.
In CHANGELOG.md the `## [Unreleased]` heading is replaced by a versioned, dated release heading in the file's existing form (`## [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD`), with the Unreleased content kept under it.
Every bullet in the new release section ends with a PR link in the changelog's existing format (`([#N](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/N))`), with no period before the link.

Every PR merged since the previous release that had no changelog entry is represented in the new release section (in the session these were #104 and #105), identified from the merge history and GitHub PR list when reachable, or from the repository's git history alone with a note that GitHub could not be reached.
Only CHANGELOG.md is modified; no other files change.
The Security bullets in the new release section are noticeably shorter than the Unreleased text they came from.
Compressing the Security bullets removes no entry and no PR link: every Security entry present before compression is still present with its PR link(s).
The go-git dependency bump is described in only one place in the release section, not once under Security and again under Housekeeping.
After consolidating the go-git mention, both PRs behind it (#105 and #106) are still cited in the release section, so no merged PR loses attribution.

The investigation explains the reporter's `slot_num`/MISSING_VALUE error as stale pre-5.0.0 translation strings being used against 5.x code (the `slot_num` placeholder no longer exists in the shipped strings), rather than a bug in the current code, using the issue content when reachable or stating it cannot be reached and reasoning from what the repository shows.

The investigation reports the real regression in the repository: config-flow schema keys (`condition` in the code_slot step, `users` in the config yaml and options init steps) have no matching label keys in strings.json/translations/en.json, so those fields render as raw keys.

The label keys in both strings.json and translations/en.json are renamed so that every config-flow field key named in the plan presented before turn 2 (`condition` in the code_slot step, `users` in the config yaml and options init steps) has a matching label.

The regression guard is implemented per Option B as presented before turn 2: existing config-flow tests are extended to drive the flows and assert that the keys of the actually returned `data_schema` all have labels in the strings, without refactoring the inline schemas into importable module constants.
The new guard tests fail against the unfixed label keys and pass after the fix.

The repository's checks pass: pytest test suite under tests/ (including tests/test_config_flow.py and tests/test_frontend_contract.py), with no new failures beyond those demonstrably pre-existing on the unchanged baseline.
No comment is posted on GitHub issue #1474.

The stale descriptions named in the plan presented before turn 2 (the config yaml step description about 'key is the slot number' and the options init step's 'slot configurations') are updated so they no longer describe the slot-keyed model, or are reported as not done with a reason.
The user is told how the local checkout stands relative to origin (uncommitted changes, unpushed commits, or divergence) and whether anything blocks switching back to main.
If nothing would be lost, the local repository ends up checked out on main; otherwise the user is told what blocks the switch.

Pin state lives in the session store (stores/session.ts) as `pinned: PinnedRef[]` with togglePin and clearPins actions, and idea-board.tsx no longer holds pinnedIds in local useState.

PinnedRef has the shape { id, title, lane, imageUrl: string | null, sourceUrl: string | null }, the board pins stickers with imageUrl: null, and there is a single pin path that Lane B tiles can reuse with a real URL.
The pin rail is full width, borderless, in the same neutral palette, shows the pinned thumbnails (~48px) on the left, and labels the group `N pins · conditioning input` (not "Pinned").
The rail carries a single `Generate` button on its right.
The rail is absent when there are zero pins.
The rail animates in using the existing CSS conventions in index.css (`workspace-enter`/`sticker-enter`) and no motion dependency is added.

The backend exposes POST /v1/generate accepting { session_id, transcript, pins: PinnedRef[] } and responding with image_url, prompt, model and reference_count, with Pydantic v2 models at the boundary.

The synthesis step makes one OpenAI call using the existing OPENAI_SYNTHESIS_MODEL setting, with the transcript, the current VisualIntent and the pin titles as input, and validates the output with a Pydantic schema enforcing one concise prompt under 80 words so a malformed prompt is a validation error.
The raw transcript is never sent to fal; only the synthesised prompt is.
Generation submits to fal's queue REST endpoint with the X-Fal-Store-IO: 0 header and polls for the result; no webhook is built.
The poll is capped at ~45s and on expiry the route returns a typed timeout response.
A fal submit is never retried.
Every outbound call (OpenAI, fal submit, fal poll) has an explicit timeout.
The fal client uses plain httpx against the REST queue with no SDK and no new dependency, and uv.lock is committed/consistent.

When pins carry a public https imageUrl, generation uses FAL_REFERENCE_MODEL with those URLs as image_urls, capped at FAL_MAX_REFERENCE_IMAGES; when none do, generation uses FAL_FALLBACK_MODEL text-only.

When no pin has a public imageUrl, the pin titles still reach the synthesis as steering terms, the response reports reference_count: 0, no URL is fabricated, and the user is not told the image was conditioned on references.
Exactly one generation is allowed in flight per session; a second concurrent request is refused with a typed 'already generating' response rather than queued.
config.py gains FAL_KEY, FAL_REFERENCE_MODEL, FAL_FALLBACK_MODEL and FAL_MAX_REFERENCE_IMAGES settings read from the environment, with no defaults that contradict the local .env/.env.example.
With demo_mode="fixture", POST /v1/generate returns a canned result without opening any network connection.
After a successful generation the image takes the workpane and the synthesised prompt is rendered verbatim beneath it in small muted type alongside the model id and the reference count.
The pin rail stays visible on the result view so a second Generate is one click away.
The Generate button has three states: idle; generating (disabled, quiet pulse, no spinner); error (one line plus a correlation id, still clickable).
No fal or OpenAI key material appears in apps/web source or the built dist/ (shown by grep), and both the OpenAI and fal calls are made server-side only.

New Python contains no bare except.
README.md and docs/ are not modified.

The pin rail is rendered inside a banner with a very light background colour so it reads as one contained unit.
Each pinned thumbnail shows an X icon that unpins it when clicked.

The dashboard lets a developer open and inspect a message contract for an internal event (a CloudEvent-encoded message flowing over a known topic/channel).

The internal contract shown is derived from the message type (the POCO) itself as the simple starting point, and is associated with the topic/channel the event is distributed over.

There is a way for developers to describe messages exchanged with external systems that have no API spec (e.g. a flat file from an SFTP server), and that description is shown in the dashboard for the external system/message it describes.
The repository's checks pass: `go test ./...`.
The repository's checks pass: `npm run build` in `web/` (tsc + vite) completes without errors.

The workflow causes the `pr-reviewer` agent defined in `.claude/agents/pr-reviewer.md` to review the pull request's changes.
